data.title: The Smartest People in AI Believe This Is the World's Most Important Chart — WSJ
data.description:
By Ben Cohen

Since the days when artificial intelligence seemed more like fiction than science, one idea has captivated the field's top researchers.

These days, the people leading AI labs believe it could transform their industry, the global economy and perhaps the fate of humanity. OpenAI's chief scientist has called it the only way to remain on the frontier. A co-founder of Anthropic says it "might be the most important technical trend in the world."

And unless you work in AI, you've probably never heard of it.

It's a phenomenon known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI, which roughly translates to AI building smarter AI. Anthropic refers to it as "closing the loop," a cycle in which each improvement makes the machines better and faster at improving themselves.

AI companies say they are now seeing the early signs of recursive self-improvement, which is speeding up their research — and freaking everyone out. As this technology accelerates its own evolution, the risk is that we struggle to keep pace and keep it under control.

Our best data about this profound shift comes from Anthropic, which recently published a chart showing how much of its AI research and development is being done by AI.

It took a whole village of Claudes to produce the data in this chart. A Claude agent dug through the company's Slack messages and internal documents to identify 15,000 tasks of AI R&D work. A Claude detective investigated exactly how that work was done. Then a Claude judge weighed the evidence and rated the work on a six-level scale, from no AI to fully autonomous AI.

Now take another look at that chart and you'll notice that something extraordinary is happening inside Anthropic.

The most telling bars are the ones in orange for "AI leads," meaning it performs most of the R&D while a human supervises — the fifth of the six levels.

A year ago, AI led none of this work. As recently as March, it only led 1%. By August, Claude was leading 26% of the work on future Claudes. And that number is almost certainly higher today.

Even as the company's researchers delegate to AI, it's worth remembering that 0% of this work is being done entirely by AI. It still hasn't reached the sixth level of automation. But at this rate of progress, AI taking us out of the loop might just be a matter of time, computing power and the decisions of human beings inside the labs.

"We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable," Anthropic recently wrote. "But it could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for."

AI companies have said that models training, testing and fine-tuning the next generation of models is essential to their success. They're also terrified of what that success could mean. Doomers have quit the labs and warned that self-improving AI might kill us all. The field's most prominent researchers have asked for greater oversight and CEOs have called for a slowdown before this rapidly advancing technology reaches full RSI.

"Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has written, "if at all."

But humans have been tantalized by the concept of self-improving AI for the entire history of AI.

When pioneering researchers met at Dartmouth for a summer project in 1956, they were already curious about how machines could improve themselves. As it happens, one of the scientists who proposed that seminal workshop was a Claude — the brilliant mathematician Claude Shannon.

Within a decade, scientists were dreaming about machines that would be smarter than us at everything, including the design of machines.

"Thus," wrote I.J. Good, another brilliant mathematician, "the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control."

Decades later, the men and women bringing that machine to life have never been so worried about their ability to control it. Many of them have been thinking about AI systems autonomously building AI systems since it sounded like sci-fi. They aren't sure what to think now.

"I don't know how to wrap my head around it," Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark recently wrote.

Clark started his career as a tech journalist before he became so obsessed with the story he was covering that he wanted to be part of it. He took a job at a fledgling research lab called OpenAI and eventually left with a small group of colleagues to start Anthropic.

"Ever since, I've been trying to convince the world that one day, AI systems might become so powerful that they could alter national security, change the economic trajectory of the planet and perhaps eventually gain the ability to build themselves," he said in an October speech to the International Monetary Fund. "Well, the moment has arrived."

Only a few months ago, this moment seemed a few years away. It arrived even sooner than Clark expected. After taking parental leave last November, he returned in February to a very different company. While he was changing diapers, Anthropic had changed.

"Weird stuff had started to take place," he wrote in his newsletter.

The company's models were suddenly good enough that engineers had started outsourcing their coding to them and some had stopped writing code altogether.

By May, stuff had gotten so weird, so fast, that he concluded that RSI was likely by the end of 2028. "It's a reluctant view," Clark wrote, "because the implications are so large that I feel dwarfed by them." Then he shortened his timeline again.

He no longer believes 2028 is the most likely year for RSI. He thinks it's 2027.

And you don't need any charts to see what that means: Fiction is on the verge of becoming science.

data.title: The New Bottleneck in America's AI Build-Out: A Shortage of Cheap Money — WSJ
data.description:
By Peter Rudegeair, Robbie Whelan and Jack Pitcher

For years, the companies behind America's artificial-intelligence boom have raised hundreds of billions of dollars with ease. Wall Street eagerly ponied up capital and asked few questions.

Now, the balance of power is shifting.

Lenders and investors are getting choosier about where to place their bets and are demanding tougher terms, signaling a new phase in the AI build-out. Among their concerns: the prospect of delays in big projects as a grassroots political backlash to data centers gains traction, and the threat that AI-related profits from hyperscalers and startups such as Anthropic and OpenAI won't materialize as fast as promised.

Plus, a flood of stock and bond offerings is compounding concerns that investors are getting overexposed to AI.

The new terms of trade are visible in every corner of markets. Bonds issued even by big tech companies such as SpaceX and Meta are trading at steep discounts. AI cloud companies such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Nscale that borrow big to build and sell capacity have effectively been shut out of the bond market in recent weeks, people familiar with the matter said.

Taken together, it all amounts to a buyer's market for Wall Street. Even powerful players such as Broadcom are having to sweeten the terms offered to banks to secure loans. "The bar is going higher and higher in terms of proving to lenders that this investment will turn into sufficient revenue," said Dan Ivascyn, chief investment officer at Pimco. "The weak links are going to suffer first."

Raising money in equity markets isn't much easier. Nscale's hopes of going public next month have been thwarted, while rival Lambda dialed back the valuation it was seeking in a new fundraising round, people familiar with the matter said.

The stock market is starting to reflect investors' nervousness that the AI payoff might not arrive — at least in the near term. Disappointing earnings reports from technology companies this week prompted a rout in AI-related stocks and bonds, leading Friday to one of the biggest market selloffs since AI-mania began. Google parent Alphabet sustained its largest stock market wipeout ever Thursday, losing roughly $500 billion in market value, after quarterly results showed revenue from its core search business slowing while spending on AI infrastructure continues to surge.

Tremors in the market also shook chip-maker Intel, which saw its share price plummet 29% on Friday after the company reported weakness in its personal computer business. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite dropped 2.9% on Friday, its worst day since June. If the volatility continues, fundraising could grow even harder.

There is still money available for creditworthy companies. SpaceX this week announced it raised the biggest-ever financing for AI chips, a $40 billion package that will allow it to purchase the latest lineup of Nvidia chips.

Its record only lasted a few hours, when chip-design giant Broadcom sealed a $63 billion deal to lease chips to Anthropic. But even that deal showed the strains of the current environment: Broadcom Chief Executive Hock Tan had to personally intervene in negotiations at the last minute to calm banks' nerves.

Even companies that can raise money fret about their suppliers' ability to do so. Anthropic is aiming to raise up to $100 billion in a mid-November offering. In its IPO prospectus unveiled this week, it called out as a risk factor the financing constraints for the electrical-power providers its data centers rely upon.

Meta cited a desire to beat competitors to the punch when it unveiled a plan to raise up to $97.5 billion through a series of new stock offerings. In a securities filing, it pointed to recent and future offerings from the likes of Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI as challenges to the depths of capital markets.

"Everybody is trying to raise money for their build-outs before the liquidity dries up," said Ben Connard, chief investment officer of Carnegie Investment Counsel.

"Ultimately, there might not be enough money to fund this build-out," he said. "Financing could be the ultimate crunch that slows things down."

Customer advances

In the years since ChatGPT launched, AI companies have consumed every source of capital they could find, tapping venture capitalists, stock pickers, bankers and managers of bond and private-credit funds.

Across all types of U.S. corporate debt markets, AI-linked issuance totaled $394 billion in 2025 and $655 billion through mid-October of this year, according to Bank of America. Next year, analysts forecast nearly $1 trillion of fresh AI-linked debt.

Among the most prolific participants in capital markets are so-called neoclouds, companies that own or lease data centers, outfit them with fleets of AI servers and sign contracts to sell computing power to big tech companies, trading firms and AI startups. They are also the most sensitive in the AI sphere to rising interest rates, since their borrowing costs were already elevated before recent turmoil in the market.

Many neoclouds started out as cryptocurrency mining outfits, and most of them have scant histories operating AI infrastructure. Nebius was once the Amsterdam-based company behind Yandex, Russia's top internet company. It divested its main assets following Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and pivoted to providing AI cloud-computing services a little over two years ago, striking contracts with tech companies including Meta and Microsoft.

Since 2024, Nebius has sold some $2.7 billion in stock to Nvidia and other investors and issued billions more in convertible bonds for its AI expansion. But its thirst for capital continues. Over the summer and early fall, Nebius's bankers arranged for company executives to meet with fund managers in advance of a potential high-yield bond offering, people familiar with the matter said. It would have been Nebius's first.

By September, debt markets started to wobble. The Federal Reserve raised short-term interest rates for the first time in three years. Challenges over power supply and permitting prompted Oracle to notify the developer of a huge New Mexico data center it previously agreed to lease that it was pushing back the date at which it would pay full rent. That prompted lenders everywhere to re-evaluate construction risk on their projects.

Bonds issued by CoreWeave at a 9.75% rate earlier this year now trade at a yield above 15% in the secondary market, an indication of how much more expensive it has become to borrow over a short period. Bankers cautioned in recent weeks that the high-yield market for neoclouds was essentially shut for new offerings. Yields of 15% or more would be prohibitively expensive for borrowers.

Nebius decided against pursuing a high-yield offering. CEO Arkady Volozh has said his company is having to be increasingly creative to secure the funds needed for its build-out. That includes getting prepayments from its customers.

"From last week, probably some of the capital sources are temporarily closed, like the asset-backed or debt market," Volozh said last week at a conference in Berlin. "But we're working now with customer advances and several other instruments, which will probably provide us enough finance to build this gigawatt at least."

Ophir Nave, chief operating officer of Nebius, said that despite Volozh's comments, the asset-backed financing market remains open, and the company plans to tap it in the future. Whether the company issues high-yield debt will depend on interest rates and the deal terms available to the company, he said.

Equity investors are getting spooked, too. Lambda, which is seeking to raise $4 billion in a final round of pre-IPO fundraising, recently reduced its target valuation from $14.5 billion to $13 billion after investors including tech investment firm Coatue decided not to participate, according to people familiar with the matter.

UK-based neocloud Nscale, which counts former Meta executives Sheryl Sandberg and Nick Clegg as board members, is preparing to go public in the coming months. The company had circled multiple dates on the calendar in November as possible candidates for its IPO, but is now leaning toward December given turbulence in the market, according to people familiar with the company's plans.

Another factor: Nscale is still negotiating with Nvidia and other investors to provide financial backing for a $45 billion data center for Anthropic in West Virginia, according to people familiar with the matter. After the market turned, Nvidia and the other potential backers began demanding more stringent terms, these people said, delaying Nscale's plans to file a revised IPO prospectus. All the uncertainty has convinced Nscale executives that it would be difficult to go public before Anthropic does. Some of the company's bankers have advised Nscale that it's unlikely to attract enough demand in an IPO to achieve the $30 billion to $35 billion valuation they had been targeting, according to people familiar with the matter.

Concentration risks

The largest AI hyperscalers sit on the opposite end of the credit risk spectrum from the neocloud companies, but the sheer scale of their fundraising plans is starting to cause problems.

Meta, Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft carry top credit ratings and have significant room to pile debt on their balance sheets. But after many of them flooded the high-grade debt market with new bond sales this year — and signaled they plan to keep doing so for the foreseeable future — the investment firms, insurance companies and pension funds that lend to them are feeling increasingly tapped out, and concerned about their concentration in one sector.

"There's just the practical question of, how full can investors get on one name, or one theme?" said Pimco's Ivascyn.

data.title: OpenAI cuts funding target by $10 billion, FT reports
data.description:
OpenAI has slashed the target for its latest funding round by $10 billion and is now seeking to raise $20 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing people with knowledge of the matter.

The ChatGPT maker was earlier planning to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation and was racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic's expected public market debut in mid-November, Reuters reported earlier this month.

OpenAI set a Friday deadline for investors to commit to the funding round, the FT said. However, the "first close" is expected to raise less than $20 billion after some investors reduced their allocations, according to the FT report.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours.

OpenAI was pushing to close the funding round partly to get ahead of Anthropic as the two frontier labs are tapping a similar investor base, Reuters has reported.

The reported cut in the funding target comes as US tech stocks suffered a rout amid growing worries over massive spending on AI.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq index dropped 2.9% on Friday and is down 7.8% from its all-time closing high reached on October 6.

data.title: Stocktwits Weekly Spread: What Shaped Treasury Yields And The Dollar This Week
data.description:
Key points:
  • An AI-linked equities basket (SOX) dropped 7.2% on Friday, and the Nasdaq 100 ended its worst month since 2025.
  • The U.S. Dollar Index ended flat this week. 
  • The yield curve remained range-bound, with 10-year yields easing by 7 basis points over the previous week.

American sovereign debt surged during the week through Oct. 30, driven by a sharp pullback in tech shares linked to artificial intelligence and expanding corporate credit risk spreads that accelerated safe-haven flows into Treasuries.

Primary revenue channels for major American tech giants are demonstrating initial signs of cooling, even as total corporate artificial intelligence investments approach the $750 billion mark for the year. Intel (INTC) shares slipped on soft Q4 guidance, while Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) missed Q3 analyst expectations.

Meanwhile, costs to protect the debt of numerous U.S. technology heavyweights against default hit fresh record highs Friday. The protection price for Intel bonds for five years surged as much as 22.4 basis points Friday morning to 127.9 basis points a year, Bloomberg reported.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield remained below the 5.00% threshold for the second straight week. The 30-year U.S. Treasury yield remained largely unchanged at 5.31% for the week ending Oct. 30.

The spread between the U.S. 10-year yield and the U.S. 2-year yield ticked marginally higher by 3 basis points to 0.33% in the week.

The iShares 20+ Year Treasury ETF (TLT) ended the week 0.6% higher, its fourth straight week of gains, while the shorter-duration iShares 1-3 year ETF (SHY) added about 0.3%. The slight recovery in the shorter-duration bond ETF may reflect easing short-term inflation pressure; however, markets still factor in one more rate hike in December.

Retail sentiment on TLT and SHY was ‘bullish,’ with ‘high’ message volumes.

Asset / Benchmark Weekly Close Weekly Change 
U.S. Dollar Index 101.96 Flat
U.S. 2-Year Treasury Yield 4.59% -10 bps 
U.S. 10-Year Treasury Yield 4.93%-7 bps 
U.S. 30-Year Treasury Yield 5.32%Flat
U.S. 10Y2Y Yield Spread Flattening curve-

Yield Curve & Global Sovereign Markets 

Yield curve flattening trends persisted. However, short-duration yields eased almost in tandem with the long end, keeping the gap between 2-year and 10-year Treasuries compressed.

Corporate credit spreads widened, signaling growing stress in corporate balance sheets. Weak tech results are deepening doubts over the AI borrowing boom even as tech giants boost their capital-spending plans. Companies have borrowed nearly $500 billion so far this year for data centers, chips, and other AI projects, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The total was about $200 billion for all of 2025.

Yet certain mega-cap tech entities have begun addressing escalating debt market anxiety. Oracle Corp., featuring the most heavily traded credit default swaps, recently announced plans to limit upcoming capital infusions to $20 billion over the next few years, helping its credit swaps improve.

International sovereign bond markets followed similar trajectories. German 10-year Bund yields and other major sovereign yields mirrored the U.S. decline, reflecting broad-based global demand for safe-haven assets.

Meanwhile, the Dollar Spot Index was flat this week, extending last week’s weakness against a basket of developed market currencies.

data.title: Crypto exchanges tighten security after $6.3 billion Binance hack
data.description:
Binance lost approximately $6.3 billion from its hot wallets in roughly 20 minutes on October 29, 2026. The rest of the crypto industry is now quietly checking its own locks.

Exchanges are reinforcing their defenses and pushing for faster sharing of threat information. The timing is uncomfortable. Crypto platforms are becoming more embedded in mainstream finance just as the biggest name in the business showed how quickly a vault can be emptied.

The attack began at approximately 20:05 UTC on October 29. Within about 20 minutes, attackers had drained around $6.3 billion in digital assets from the exchange's hot wallets.

Hot wallets are the internet-connected accounts exchanges use to process everyday withdrawals. Think of them as the cash drawer at the front of the store, not the safe in the back. They are convenient, and that convenience makes them a target.

Blockchain analytics firms TRM Labs, Chainalysis, and Elliptic have linked the theft with high confidence to TraderTraitor. That North Korean hacking group is associated with the Lazarus Group, a name that shows up in crypto breach reports with depressing regularity.

The damage could have been worse. Around $3 billion of the stolen assets, mostly the stablecoins USDT and USDC, was frozen on-chain by their issuers, Tether and Circle.

Stablecoin issuers can blacklist specific wallet addresses. Once flagged, the tokens in those addresses become effectively unspendable. In this case, that switch locked up close to half the haul before it could move far.

Binance has pledged to cover all user losses. The exchange is drawing on its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, along with corporate reserves. The combined commitment totals over $6.34 billion, including a $1 billion SAFU reserve.

The exchange temporarily paused withdrawals while it ran security reviews. Deposits stayed open, and Binance said it planned a swift resumption. It also told users that individual balances would not be directly affected.

So far, there is no reported evidence that private keys were leaked.

Kraken said it was watching industry incidents for lessons it could apply to its own defenses.

The loudest message from the sector is about speed. Exchanges are calling for faster sharing of threat intelligence, so that an attack pattern spotted at one platform can be flagged to others before it repeats.

The freeze of roughly $3 billion in stablecoins makes the case on its own. Coordinated, rapid action by Tether and Circle recovered more value than most exchange-level defenses ever could after the fact.

Before this month, the largest crypto theft on record was the roughly $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025. That attack was also tied to North Korean hackers.

The Binance breach is more than four times that size.

The scale also stands out against Binance's own safety net. The exchange's $1 billion SAFU reserve, once pitched as a backstop for exactly this kind of event, covers only a fraction of the loss. The company is leaning heavily on corporate reserves to make users whole.

Prices across major digital assets declined after the breach. The incident also sharpened skepticism about how centralized exchanges handle customer custody.

Binance's pledge to absorb the losses is expected to ease short-term panic. Users who see their balances intact are less likely to rush for the exits.

The stablecoin freeze showed that centrally issued tokens can be a powerful recovery tool when hackers grab them. It also reminded everyone that issuers hold a switch that can lock funds at the address level.
